title: Holiday Parenting Plans in Colorado: Review Your Schedule Early

content.rendered:
Holiday parenting plans in Colorado can become complicated when parents need to coordinate Thanksgiving, winter break, and family travel. Reviewing your existing parenting plan early can help you understand the schedule, clarify expectations, and reduce the risk of unnecessary conflicts during the holiday season.

Review Your Existing Parenting Plan Early

The first step in preparing for the holidays is reviewing your current parenting plan and seeing what it says about holidays.  Does your calendar reflect the court order?

Parenting plans should include specific provisions for holidays, school breaks, and special occasions. Most parenting plans also require regular communication by the parents about the children.

Before making unilateral plans to fly to North Dakota to spend the holidays with Great Aunt Mildred and her 300 head of cattle that need the whole family to care for, review your actual court-approved parenting plan and double check a few things:

  • Which holidays are specifically addressed?
  • Does the parenting plan alternate certain holidays each year?
  • Are there specific exchange times or locations?
  • How are school breaks handled?
  • Does the plan address travel? Do you need to provide the itinerary to your ex for this fun holiday trip to a cattle ranch in North Dakota when it’s 40 below zero and Great Aunt Mildred’s idea of how to create fun childhood holiday memories is getting your screen-addicted teens, who may or may not be vegan, up at 4:00 am to feed hundreds of head cattle?
  • Are there provisions that may affect your awesome plans in North Dakota this year?
  • Is “winter break” defined by the school calendar, or specific dates and which school district’s calendar applies?

Read your parenting plan.

If your plan alternates holidays by even and odd years, remember that 2026 is an even year. Check now which parent has Thanksgiving (November 26) and each part of winter break.

Start the Conversation Now

Pick up the phone and do something old-fashioned and call your ex, or invite them to coffee and just hammer out the schedule face to face.  Have the parenting plan in front of you.

Early communication does not guarantee that parents will agree on every detail, but it gives you more time to figure things out together before they become urgent.

Keep Your Children’s Needs at the Center of the Plan

Holiday schedules can be busy for everyone, especially children.

When discussing parenting arrangements, it can be helpful to consider how the proposed schedule will affect your children—but DON’T discuss it with them first! Please.

Once you have the plan in place, including any AGREED UPON deviations, let the children know. That’s the way functioning adult parents do it.  Kids can weigh in too, but remember, Colorado courts only consider a child’s wishes when the child is mature enough to express reasoned and independent preferences (C.R.S. § 14-10-124(1.5)(a)). And no court is going to have a kid testify about anything with very rare exceptions.  Plus those wishes are one factor among many. And PLEASE, don’t be so self-centered that you ask your kids to choose between their parents or transmit messages about parenting time. Just stop. If you can’t skip the trip to see Great Aunt Mildred and her hundreds of head of cattle and instead get into intensive one-on-one counseling to learn how to parent your kids better. There’s no shame in it and everyone needs to keep learning how to be better human beings anyway. I know it sounds a little harsh, but I’ve seen a few things in my 27 years of practicing law.

Make Travel Plans Clear

Holiday travel can create additional challenges when parents live in different locations or have extended family outside Colorado.

Before making travel arrangements, parents should provide detailed itineraries including airlines, flight numbers, times, transportation and where the kids will be staying and with whom.  If you are going outside the country, you’ll need passports and a travel consent letter.

Keep in mind that an informal agreement between parents does not change your court order. If the agreement falls apart, the court order is what will be enforced. If a change is meant to last beyond this holiday season, it may need to be formalized with the court.

Consider Mediation When Parents Cannot Agree

If parents are having difficulty resolving a holiday scheduling dispute, and you decide to file something in court, the court will order mediation. A neutral mediator can help parents facilitate an agreement quickly.
